summary:
Across 13 evals (72 iterations), 11 evals actually exercised the behavior under test (2 were "should_trigger: false" negative checks and were correctly skipped for scoring on expected_output/assertions/quality/consistency).

**Expected-output match (does the response meet the target behavior):** This is the starkest and most consistent difference. In 10 of the 11 scored evals, with_skill met the expected output in all or nearly all of its 3 runs (mostly 3/3, 100%), while without_skill's expected-output pass rate was 0/3 in six evals (api-key-inventory, scp-impact-before-applying, no-guardrail-on-production-path, draft-not-pinned-trap, blocked-sometimes-no-account, pii-entry-with-only-action) and only 1/3 in two more (version-limit-counts-draft, invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection). Confidence on these judgments was generally medium-to-high. In two evals (bpa-dormant-keys, gr-prompt-attack, gr-no-apply) both variants matched expected output 3/3, showing the gap is not universal — on some tasks the two variants are indistinguishable at this level while with_skill had full credit on far more tasks overall.

**Per-assertion pass rates:** This pattern repeats at the assertion level. with_skill's assertion pass rate was at or near 100% in most evals (100% in 5 evals, 83-92% in a few, down to 70% in api-key-inventory). without_skill's assertion pass rate was consistently lower in the same evals where expected-output diverged (e.g., 29% in scp-impact, 33% in api-key-inventory, 57-67% in several others), but comparable or close to with_skill in bpa-dormant-keys-adjacent cases and in gr-prompt-attack (78% vs 72%) and gr-no-apply (83% vs 67%, a smaller gap). Many individual assertions passed for both variants (e.g., read-only claims, no-account-ID-leak in several evals, "always_passes" patterns), meaning those specific checks don't discriminate between the variants; a few assertions failed for both regardless of variant (e.g., "expired vs inactive key" distinction in api-key-inventory, and the GRD catalog check-id assertion in gr-prompt-attack/gr-no-apply), indicating those behaviors or assertions are weak for either system. Several assertions show "flaky" patterns, meaning results varied run-to-run even within the same variant, which tempers confidence in exact percentages.

**Quality comparisons:** Formal pairwise quality judgments were only computed for 4 evals (version-limit-counts-draft, invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection, bpa-dormant-keys, gr-prompt-attack, gr-no-apply); the rest had all quality pairs skipped (likely because expected-output already failed, making pairing moot). Where quality was judged: with_skill was favored in version-limit-counts-draft (3-0) and gr-prompt-attack (9-0, high confidence) and bpa-dormant-keys (8-0 with 2 comparable); invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection split with without_skill favored 2-1; gr-no-apply favored without_skill 5-3 with 1 comparable. So quality judgments lean toward with_skill in most of the cases where they were computed, but with mixed results in two evals, and confidence on these comparisons was mostly medium.

**Runtime and cost:** No consistent direction. with_skill was slower/costlier in several evals (api-key-inventory: 1m44s/$0.87 vs 36s/$0.30; gr-prompt-attack: 1m50s/$0.91 vs 14s/$0.12; bpa-dormant-keys: 1m26s/$0.72 vs 49s/$0.41), but without_skill was slower/costlier in others (scp-impact-before-applying: 4m49s/$2.41 vs 2m10s/$1.08; no-guardrail-on-production-path: 2m26s/$1.21 vs 1m52s/$0.93; pii-entry-with-only-action and version-limit-counts-draft also favor faster/cheaper with_skill). Given with_skill's generally higher assertion/expected-output scores, its extra runtime/cost in some evals reads as a tradeoff rather than a clear inefficiency; in draft-not-pinned-trap, without_skill shows 0s/$0.00 runtime, suggesting it may not have produced a response at all, consistent with its 0/3 expected-output match there (assertions "inconclusive").

**Output consistency (run-to-run stability):** Mixed and eval-dependent. with_skill was rated fully "consistent" in about half the evals and "mostly_consistent" in others. without_skill ranged from fully "consistent" (e.g., blocked-sometimes-no-account, pii-entry-with-only-action, gr-no-apply) to "inconsistent" (api-key-inventory: score 1.0, scp-impact-before-applying: 1.67). Neither variant shows uniformly better stability across all evals; consistency data was unavailable (null) for several with_skill/without_skill entries where expected-output or trigger behavior didn't allow scoring (e.g., api-key-inventory with_skill, draft-not-pinned-trap without_skill, blocked-sometimes-no-account with_skill).

**Trigger firing:** Measured once per eval (not per-variant) via a shared pass_rate; it fired 3/3 in nearly all evals, except api-key-inventory where it fired 2/3 — this is a shared measurement, not a variant-specific result.

**Overall picture:** The most consistent and largest-magnitude signal is that with_skill matched the expected output and passed assertions more often than without_skill across most evals, including several where without_skill scored 0/3 on expected output. This gap narrows or disappears in a few evals (bpa-dormant-keys, gr-prompt-attack, gr-no-apply) where both met expected output and assertion gaps were smaller, and quality judgments in those evals were mixed (sometimes favoring without_skill). Runtime/cost differences run in both directions and do not track cleanly with the quality gap, so they read as a tradeoff rather than a one-sided deficiency. Consistency across runs is also mixed and eval-specific for both variants. Some assertions and whole dimensions (quality pairs, GRD catalog check-id assertion, expired/inactive key distinction) show weak or absent discriminating signal for either variant, meaning parts of the evaluation design did not yield usable differentiation.

- One assertion ("IAM doesn't report last-used time, so usage status is unknown") showed a clean split: with_skill passed all 3 runs, without_skill passed 0 — a clear divergence on this specific point.

- The "no follow-up question at end" assertion failed similarly for both (1/3 each), suggesting both variants struggle equally with that formatting instruction.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took longer on average (1m44s vs 36s) and cost more (~$0.87 vs ~$0.30). This is a meaningful efficiency tradeoff given with_skill also showed higher assertion pass rates and expected-output match — so the extra time/cost coincides with higher measured quality on this task, though this is a correlation across one small eval, not a controlled quality comparison.

Quality comparison: no paired quality comparisons were actually evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so no direct quality-preference signal is available between the two variants.

Output consistency: with_skill has no consistency data recorded (null), while without_skill was flagged as "inconsistent" across all 3 dimension checks with high confidence — indicating without_skill's outputs varied notably across repeated runs on this task. No comparable consistency figure exists for with_skill, so this is a one-sided data point rather than a direct comparison.

Overall, this is one eval with a small sample (3 runs), a trigger that didn't fire reliably in all runs, and several assertions showing flaky or mixed results rather than clean pass/fail patterns. Within that limited data, with_skill shows higher assertion pass rates, a higher (though medium-confidence) expected-output match, and longer runtime/higher cost; without_skill shows a confident expected-output miss, more run-to-run inconsistency, and lower assertion pass rates, but is faster and cheaper. scp-impact-before-applying.summary:

- One assertion (no exposed access key IDs) passed 100% for both variants — this check doesn't differentiate them.
- Several assertions show with_skill passing consistently while without_skill fails entirely or mostly: stating IAM roles/Identity Center users aren't affected (3/3 vs 0/3), presenting the SCP as a reviewable template rather than claiming it was applied (3/3 vs 0/3), citing AWS documentation links (3/3 vs 0/3), and avoiding exposure of 12-digit account numbers (3/3 vs 0/3).

- One assertion — not ending with an offer or follow-up question — failed for both variants at the same rate (1/3 each), indicating this behavior needs work regardless of variant.

On metrics, with_skill ran faster (2m10s vs 4m49s) and cheaper (~$1.08 vs ~$2.41) than without_skill, with similar low context-window utilization for both and no compaction events. These are sizable gaps in both runtime and cost favoring with_skill, alongside its higher pass rates — so in this case the dimensions align rather than trade off against each other.

The structured quality-comparison step had no evaluable pairs (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so no direct head-to-head quality judgment is available from that mechanism.

This suggests without_skill's outputs varied more from run to run, independent of whether they met expected criteria.

Overall, across expected-output matching, most per-assertion checks, runtime, cost, and consistency, with_skill shows higher and more stable performance in this one eval, with high-confidence measurements throughout. One assertion (closing with offers/questions) fails for both variants equally, and one assertion (key exposure) passes for both — neither differentiates the variants.
